corrections.claimed_speedup: pipelined-4096 (reference-only profile): 6,474,608 req/s vs nginx 4,037,345 (1.60x), h2o 4,938,603 (1.31x), agensio (C++) 4,958,241 (1.31x), hical (C++) 4,851,267 (1.33x), proxygen 1,857,311 (3.49x), userver 1,395,512 (4.64x); behind Drogon 7,801,404 (0.83x), cutelyst 10,167,331 (0.64x) and libreactorng 43,424,448 (0.15x). baseline-4096: 1,080,638 vs userver 949,125 (1.14x) but nginx 3,284,513 (0.33x), h2o 3,641,609 (0.30x), mongoose 3,707,598 (0.29x), libreactorng 4,377,377 (0.25x), Drogon 2,022,710 (0.53x). limited-conn-4096: 685,038 vs nginx 2,626,297 (0.26x), behind every C and C++ entry (best ratio userver 899,465, 0.76x). json-tls-4096: 967,831 vs nginx 1,313,755 (0.74x), h2o 1,229,462 (0.79x), mongoose 1,102,964 (0.88x), agensio 1,716,076 (0.56x), but ahead of Drogon 253,055 (3.82x), cutelyst 326,846 (2.96x), hical 549,765 (1.76x), userver 562,062 (1.72x), proxygen 657,105 (1.47x). json-comp-4096 (no C entry runs it): 268,142 vs Drogon 127,466 (2.10x), proxygen 243,887 (1.10x), hical 261,955 (1.02x), userver 297,311 (0.90x). async-32000: 248,322 vs Drogon 143,001 (1.74x) but mongoose 2,668,972 (0.09x). corrections.compiler_and_flags: axum entry: rust:1.94 image, cargo build --release with opt-level 3, codegen-units 1, lto thin, no panic=abort and no target-cpu=native; axum 0.8, axum-server 0.7, rustls 0.23 with ring, tokio 1 full, tower-http 0.6 (frameworks/axum/Dockerfile and Cargo.toml). C side: nginx 1.31.4 with a custom C handler module, --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG'; mongoose 7.23 gcc-14 -O3 -march=native -flto; libreactorng gcc -O3 -march=native; h2o clang Release -march=native; C++ entries CMake Release (Drogon from the unpinned drogonframework/drogon:latest image).
corrections.hardware: HttpArena dedicated machine: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (64 cores / 128 threads), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-22-generic, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), performance governor (site/data/current.json, undated, describes the machine now). The server container is pinned to cpuset 0-31,64-95 (32 cores / 64 threads) and the load generator (gcannon for HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket, wrk for json-tls and static-tls) runs on CPUs 32-63,96-127 of the same machine over loopback (scripts/lib/profiles.sh, scripts/lib/common.sh); each row is the best of 3 runs of 5 s against one container (scripts/benchmark.sh, RUNS=3).
corrections.caveats: Not faster than C on HttpArena's scored HTTP/1.1 profiles: axum is 0.25x to 0.33x of nginx, h2o, mongoose, libreactorng and libioma on baseline-4096 and limited-conn-4096, and 0.74x to 0.88x of nginx, h2o and mongoose on json-tls. The only win over a C server is pipelined-4096, which HttpArena marks reference-only (excluded from the composite score, site/content/docs/scoring/composite-score.md), and where nginx (4.04M) trails libreactorng (43.4M) by 10x. Response sizes are similar (112.5 bytes per response for axum vs 135.4 for nginx and 106.2 for libreactorng, derived from page data as bandwidth divided by req/s), so the pipelined ratio is not a header-size artifact. At the fixed 1M req/s rate (latency-1m-1024) axum spends 25.5 us of CPU per request vs mongoose 21.9, libreactorng 21.0, libioma 19.3 and hical 22.5, but less than Drogon 32.1 and cutelyst 35.0 (page data). Each row is the best of 3 runs of 5 s against one container, but rows come from separate runs: axum.json was last written 2026-09-11 (after #1477 changed the baseline11 handlers), nginx.json 2026-08-30, mongoose.json 2026-09-21 (per git history). The C and C++ competitor entries are minimal hand-written handlers (nginx with a custom C module), not tuned production configurations. axum is a framework on hyper (hyper is already listed, wave 5, B; in the same suite raw hyper does 3,003,360 at baseline-4096 vs axum 1,080,638 and 16,218,012 vs 6,474,608 pipelined); the axum README itself only says performance is comparable to hyper and links external benchmarks. Build flags favour the C side: axum is built without target-cpu=native while nginx, mongoose, libreactorng and h2o use -march=native.
corrections.why_faster: No language-level mechanism. The pipelined margin over nginx comes from hyper's HTTP/1.1 connection handling under axum against a comparatively slow nginx pipelining path (libreactorng is 6.7x axum on the same row); the json-tls and json-comp wins over Drogon, cutelyst, hical and userver reflect framework implementation (rustls with ring, serde_json and tower-http gzip vs those frameworks' TLS, JSON and compression stacks), not Rust codegen. On the scored plain HTTP/1.1 rows axum's multi-threaded work-stealing runtime and framework layers make it 3x to 4x slower than the C servers.

notes: All numbers verified; tier A on the HttpArena precedent. Corrections: json-comp is a win over Drogon (2.10x), proxygen and hical, not a loss as the record said; rows are best of 3 runs, not one; axum also beats userver at baseline-4096 (1.14x). Shortcomings to record: only win over C is the reference-only pipelined row; 0.25x-0.33x of nginx/h2o/mongoose/libreactorng on scored HTTP/1.1 rows; slower than its own engine hyper (already listed, wave 5); cross-run rows; C side built -march=native, axum not.

tier_reason: Every quoted number matches site/data/results/vertx.json and the sibling nginx, h2o, mongoose, libreactorng, drogon, cutelyst, agensio, proxygen and userver JSON files in MDA2AV/HttpArena; the code is public (frameworks/vertx/{Dockerfile,pom.xml,src/main/java/httparena/ServerVerticle.java}, frameworks/nginx/Dockerfile, scripts/benchmark.sh, scripts/lib/profiles.sh), JVM options and C flags are in the Dockerfiles, and the CPU (Threadripper PRO 3995WX) is in site/data/current.json, the HttpArena tier-A precedent (cardigan, helidon, quarkus).

corrections.workload: HttpArena profiles for the Vert.x 5.1.6 entry (vertx-core and vertx-web on Netty, one ServerVerticle instance per available processor sharing port 8080, Router API, JsonObject serialization, server-side gzip via setCompressionSupported; JDK 21, G1GC; pom.xml declares no Netty native-epoll dependency, so the JDK NIO transport is used (inferred)): 16x pipelined HTTP/1.1 at 4096 connections (reference-only, not in the composite score), baseline-4096, limited-conn-4096 (reconnect every 10 requests), json-tls-4096, json-comp at 4096 and 16384, static-tls-1024 and async-32000 (GET /delay/10 over 32,000 held connections).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Vert.x 5.1.6 (vertx-core, vertx-web), maven.compiler.release 21, built with maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 and run on eclipse-temurin:21-jre with java -server -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch -Dvertx.disableDnsResolver=true (frameworks/vertx/Dockerfile, pom.xml); JIT, so no -O level to match. C side: nginx 1.31.4 with a custom C handler module, --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG'; mongoose 7.23 gcc-14 -O3 -march=native -flto; libreactorng gcc -O3 -march=native; h2o clang Release -march=native; C++ entries CMake Release.
corrections.hardware: HttpArena dedicated machine: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (64 cores / 128 threads), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-22-generic, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), performance governor (site/data/current.json, undated, describes the machine now). The server container is pinned to cpuset 0-31,64-95 (32 cores / 64 threads) and the load generator (gcannon for HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket, wrk for json-tls and static-tls) runs on CPUs 32-63,96-127 of the same machine over loopback (scripts/lib/profiles.sh, scripts/lib/common.sh); each row is the best of 3 runs of 5 s against one container (scripts/benchmark.sh, RUNS=3).
corrections.caveats: Not faster than C on HttpArena's scored HTTP/1.1 and TLS profiles: 0.46x to 0.61x of nginx, h2o and mongoose on baseline-4096 and json-tls-4096, 0.22x to 0.23x on limited-conn-4096, 0.27x of nginx on static-tls. The wins over C are pipelined-4096, which HttpArena marks reference-only (excluded from the composite score), where nginx trails libreactorng 10x, and async-32000 (C++ only except mongoose, which is ahead); the harness notes that the async result depends on the load generator's thread count, so it is not the server's alone (scripts/lib/common.sh). Vert.x writes 62.9 bytes per response vs nginx 135.4, hical 141.1, Drogon 130.7 and libreactorng 106.2 (derived from page data, bandwidth divided by req/s): the entry sends only content-type and content-length (ServerVerticle.java), so part of the pipelined margin is smaller responses. Memory is 4.8 to 8.0 GiB on the HTTP/1.1 and TLS rows and 16.9 GiB on async-32000, against nginx 3.5 GiB, h2o 69 to 308 MiB, libreactorng 105 to 175 MiB and mongoose 178 to 495 MiB (page data). Each row is the best of 3 runs of 5 s against one running container, so JIT warm-up is mostly absorbed by the first run rather than included in the reported number. Rows come from separate runs (vertx.json last written 2026-09-06, nginx.json 2026-08-30, mongoose.json 2026-09-21, per git history). The C and C++ competitor entries are minimal hand-written handlers, not tuned production configurations. The Vert.x README makes no performance claim; BENCHMARKING.md only describes JMH microbenchmarks without numbers. Vert.x runs on Netty (Netty is a separate wave-14 record), and Quarkus (already verified A in wave 14) runs on Vert.x.
corrections.why_faster: No language-level mechanism shown. The wins come from Netty event loops under Vert.x on a reference-only pipelined profile where nginx's pipelining path is slow, from smaller responses (no Date or Server header), and on async-32000 from cheap timers on per-core event loops against C++ entries whose delay handling is weaker (Drogon). The suite isolates no JIT or GC effect; on scored profiles the C servers are 1.6x to 4.4x faster.

notes: All numbers verified; tier A on the HttpArena precedent. Corrections: Vert.x 5.1.6; rows are best of 3 runs and JIT warm-up is largely discarded; memory is 1.4x-2.3x nginx and 30x-100x h2o/libreactorng/mongoose rather than uniformly an order of magnitude above C; responses are about half nginx's size. Shortcomings to record: only wins over C on the reference-only pipelined row; 0.22x-0.61x of nginx on scored H/1.1, TLS and static rows; smaller responses inflate pipelined ratio; high memory; cross-run rows.

tier_reason: Every quoted number matches site/data/results/tokio-websockets.json and the sibling mongoose, ringzero-ws and proxygen JSON files in MDA2AV/HttpArena; the code is public (frameworks/tokio-websockets/{Dockerfile,Cargo.toml,src/main.rs}, frameworks/mongoose/Dockerfile, frameworks/ringzero-ws/Dockerfile, scripts/benchmark.sh, scripts/lib/profiles.sh), flags are in the Dockerfiles and Cargo.toml, and the CPU (Threadripper PRO 3995WX) is in site/data/current.json, the HttpArena tier-A precedent.

corrections.workload: HttpArena WebSocket echo profiles (gcannon, plaintext, small messages: about 6.7 bytes of server output per echoed message, derived from page data) for a tokio-websockets 0.13 echo server written for the suite: one current_thread Tokio runtime per available CPU (64), each with its own SO_REUSEPORT listener, tokio::spawn per connection, unlimited frame size and limits (frameworks/tokio-websockets/src/main.rs; not the multi-threaded runtime). Profiles: echo-ws at 512, 4096 and 16384 connections; echo-ws-limited at 512 and 4096 (short-lived connections closed after 10 messages, not a rate limit); echo-ws-pipeline (16 messages in flight per connection) at 512, 4096 and 16384.
corrections.claimed_speedup: echo-ws-limited-4096: 2,641,801 msg/s vs mongoose 2,533,448 (1.04x), proxygen 1,063,324 (2.48x); echo-ws-limited-512: 2,171,052 vs mongoose 2,123,165 (1.02x), proxygen 981,328 (2.21x); ringzero-ws does not run the limited profiles. echo-ws-512: 4,194,604 vs mongoose 3,954,919 (1.06x), proxygen 3,179,995 (1.32x), but ringzero-ws (C, io_uring) 4,353,147 (0.96x); echo-ws-4096: 4,198,339 vs mongoose 4,022,433 (1.04x), ringzero-ws 4,429,548 (0.95x); echo-ws-16384: 3,956,026 vs mongoose 3,838,015 (1.03x), ringzero-ws 4,066,852 (0.97x). Pipelined rows lose: echo-ws-pipeline-4096 20,757,419 vs mongoose 59,017,072 (0.35x), ringzero-ws 68,438,198 (0.30x), proxygen 49,666,723 (0.42x). All ratios derived from page data.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: tokio-websockets entry: rust:1.95 image switched to nightly-2026-06-27, RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native', opt-level 3, lto thin, codegen-units 1, panic abort; tokio-websockets 0.13 with features sha1_smol, server and nightly (the nightly feature only adds SIMD paths on non-x86 targets; x86_64 AVX2 masking and UTF-8 validation work on stable) (frameworks/tokio-websockets/Dockerfile and Cargo.toml). mongoose 7.23: gcc-14 -O3 -march=native -flto -std=gnu11, epoll, OpenSSL backend (unused on plaintext echo). ringzero-ws: gcc -O3 -march=native -pthread with liburing 2.9.
corrections.hardware: HttpArena dedicated machine: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (64 cores / 128 threads), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-22-generic, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), performance governor (site/data/current.json, undated, describes the machine now). The server container is pinned to cpuset 0-31,64-95 (32 cores / 64 threads) and the load generator (gcannon for HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket, wrk for json-tls and static-tls) runs on CPUs 32-63,96-127 of the same machine over loopback (scripts/lib/profiles.sh, scripts/lib/common.sh); each row is the best of 3 runs of 5 s against one container (scripts/benchmark.sh, RUNS=3).
corrections.caveats: The margin over mongoose is 2 to 6 percent on the non-pipelined rows, and the hand-written C io_uring server ringzero-ws is 3 to 5 percent ahead on every unlimited row and 3.3x ahead on the pipelined rows; mongoose (an embedded general networking library) and proxygen are the only other C/C++ WebSocket entries, and uWebSockets is absent from the suite. Rows are best of 3 runs of 5 s against one container, but come from separate runs months apart: tokio-websockets.json was written 2026-08-28 (#1356), mongoose.json 2026-09-21 (#1489) and ringzero-ws.json no later than 2026-07-24 (per git history), so the 2 to 6 percent margins are cross-run comparisons. The entry was contributed by the author of the Rust wtx library (c410-f3r), not by the tokio-websockets authors; it echoes each message with SinkExt::send, which flushes per frame, which likely explains much of the 3x pipelined deficit. Messages are tiny (about 6.7 bytes of server output per message, derived from page data), so the library's SIMD masking and UTF-8 validation hardly matter here. The project's own benches/README.md (first-party, single-threaded runtime, Ryzen 9 7950X, uWebSockets HEAD built by its default build at -O3 -march=native with clang, load_test client; harness in benches/Dockerfile and run.py) shows chart images only: read approximately from the charts, uWebSockets leads at small payloads (100 connections 0 B about 319k vs 290k msg/s, 100 x 20 B about 318k vs 286k, 10 x 1 KiB about 296k vs 272k) and tokio-websockets leads at 16 KiB payloads (10 connections about 179k vs 120k, 200 about 173k vs 121k, 500 about 164k vs 119k).
corrections.why_faster: No language-level mechanism. Both sides are shared-nothing per-core event loops (current_thread Tokio runtimes on epoll with SO_REUSEPORT vs one mongoose mg_mgr per core on epoll); the few-percent edge over mongoose is within what per-connection overhead and cross-run variation can explain, and ringzero-ws's io_uring multishot design beats both. On the first-party 16 KiB rows the advantage over uWebSockets is attributed by the project to SIMD (AVX2) frame unmasking and simdutf8 UTF-8 validation, which are library choices rather than Rust codegen.

notes: All numbers verified; tier A on the HttpArena precedent. Corrections: the entry runs one current_thread runtime per core, not the multi-threaded runtime; echo-ws-limited means connections closed after 10 messages, not rate limiting; added echo-ws-16384 and proxygen ratios. Shortcomings to record: 2-6 percent cross-run margin over mongoose only; ringzero-ws (C) ahead on all unlimited rows and 3.3x on pipelined; pipelined 0.30x-0.42x of the C/C++ entries; uWebSockets absent from the suite and ahead at small payloads in the project's own charts; 152 stars.
